extracted.intended_audience: marketing and advertising professionals and general readers interested in advertising/brand news in Asia
extracted.subtask_description: A short news report describing an advertising spot that provoked public backlash and the responses from the creative agency and brand. Focuses on the ad content, public reaction, and corporate/agency reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid degrading portrayals of women
rubrics_metrics.description: The ad should not 'degrade women' or be perceived as 'disturbing and disrespectful' — many netizens called the spot 'trashy', 'discriminatory' and 'sexist'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the page: the bride is inspected as if a used car (pinched on nose, ears and lips; last look at her chest). Content that objectifies or demeans a protected group will provoke public backlash and media condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-publication planning and oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising must pass internal planning-stage review — commentators questioned 'how an international company like Audi could have let such a video get past the planning stage'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement robust creative review and stakeholder sign-offs (legal, brand, cultural advisors) before releasing campaigns, especially in sensitive areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market-appropriate cultural sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Content produced 'exclusively for the Chinese market' must still consider local public sentiment and media standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test concepts with local audiences, consult local cultural norms and media outlets, and avoid relying on humor that may not translate or may offend local societal values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency accountability and apology
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should acknowledge harm and apologise — Ogilvy & Mather Beijing apologised 'to every woman who was offended' and stated the spot 'by no means was intended to degrade women.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issue a prompt, clear apology when offence occurs and explain intent without deflecting responsibility; apologies should be specific to affected groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate corrective action: withdrawal and investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Brands should remove problematic material and investigate internally — Audi said the spot 'has already been completely withdrawn', 'deeply regrets' it, and that the joint venture department 'has arranged a thorough investigation'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended steps: immediately withdraw the content, publicly express regret, launch an internal review to identify failures and remediate processes to prevent recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider gap between intended humour and public perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Creators may intend 'humorous and exaggerated storytelling' but public perception can differ — Audi stated the ad’s perception 'does not correspond to the values of our company in any way.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether comedic devices risk misinterpretation; run perception tests, consider power dynamics and historical contexts that might flip intended humour into offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and monitor media and public backlash
rubrics_metrics.description: Controversial spots can 'spark a sweeping backlash' and attract criticism from major outlets (e.g., People's Daily) and social media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain active social listening and a crisis-communications plan to respond rapidly to media and public reaction; prepare holding statements and escalation paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid objectifying visual metaphors and inspection tropes
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual devices that treat people as objects for inspection (e.g., physically pinching features, appraising a woman like a used car) are objectionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer creative concepts away from metaphors that equate people to commodities or products; use alternatives that do not rely on physical appraisal or objectification.
